raw_response:
I'm a 59-year-old farmer with middle school education. I've been farming 65 mu in Quzhou for 25 years. I know this land well — what the soil is like in each plot, where the low spots hold water, and which varieties have held up through the dry springs we've had lately. With just three of us at home, I hire plenty of seasonal labor, especially at harvest and planting time when everything happens at once.

My backbone is the 38 mu of wheat-maize double cropping. That's what keeps us fed and pays the basic bills. I'll plant winter wheat in early October — I use a reliable improved variety, not the newest thing on the market but one I trust. The extension people say 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I've tried that and on my land 18 kg gives me a safer yield. I put compound fertilizer down before planting as my base, then topdress with urea at jointing. I'll irrigate three times: winter irrigation, jointing, and grain filling. Pumping isn't cheap — the meter runs fast — but I lost too much yield in that dry year ten years ago. I'd rather pay for water than risk a bad wheat crop. I expect about 480 kg per mu.

For summer maize, the window after wheat harvest is brutal — sometimes five days, maybe a week if I'm lucky. I hire a custom operator with a no-till planter to get the maize in fast after the combine leaves the field. Hybrid seed, about 55 yuan per mu. Two fertilizer applications — base at planting, then urea at the big trumpet stage. Two irrigations should do it unless we get a real drought. I usually see about 520 kg per mu.

The other 27 mu is where I try to make money. Twelve mu of watermelon — I plant in late April with plastic mulch. Watermelons eat fertilizer and drink water like nothing else. I spread chicken manure plus compound fertilizer as base, then topdress twice when the fruits are setting. Six irrigations through the season. I hire a crew for planting and another for harvest — it's too much for my family. If prices are good, those 12 mu pay better than the wheat-maize. I hope for 3,500 kg per mu.

Ten mu of autumn cabbage, planted in late July. It's steady — not exciting, but the village broker always buys it. Hybrid variety, two fertilizer applications, four irrigations. The main work is at harvest, hauling those heavy heads out.

Three mu of chili, transplanted in early May. Chilis need picking again and again, so that's labor all summer. My wife and I do the early picks, but I hire workers for the main harvests in August and September. Plastic mulch saves me a lot of weeding trouble.

Two mu of stevia — that's a contract crop for a processing company. The price is fixed, so there's no upside, but no downside either. I plant in late April and harvest three times through the summer. It's easy money if you don't count your own labor.

This year fertilizer prices are still high, so I'm not increasing my rates, but I'm not cutting back either. Last year was decent, so I have some cash. In 25 years I've learned that skimping on fertilizer to save a few hundred yuan can cost you thousands in yield. I keep a cash reserve for emergencies — my daughter might need something, or the pump might break. All in all, I'll need about 68,000 yuan for seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, irrigation, and hired labor.
